"He'll Have to Go" is a song recorded on October 15, 1959, by Jim Reeves. The song, released in the fall of 1959, went on to become a hit on both the country and pop charts early in 1960.

sections.heading: Background
sections.wikitext:
The song is about a man who is talking by telephone to the woman he loves, when he realizes that another man is with her. The song was written by the husband-and-wife team of [[Joe Allison|Joe]] and Audrey Allison, and was inspired by a phone conversation between them in which they had trouble making themselves understood. Because of background noise and Audrey Allison's naturally soft voice, her husband had to ask her to put her mouth very close to the receiver.<ref>Gilbert, Bob and [[Gary Theroux]], "The Top Ten: 1956-Present," Pop Record Research, Fireside Books, Simon & Schuster, New York. 1982 ({{ISBN|0-671-43215-X}}).</ref> That led her to pen the song's first line.

Reeves recorded the song after listening to the original version of it by singer Billy Brown. When Brown's version attracted little attention, Reeves felt free to record his own. It was released to country radio as the [[A-side and B-side|B-side]] of "In a Mansion Stands My Love", which some music executives considered a stronger song. However, "Mansion" failed to catch on, and disc jockeys began playing the B-side, instead.<ref>Gilbert and Theroux, "The Top Ten."</ref> Before long, "He'll Have to Go" became a huge country and pop hit. Several [[rhythm and blues]] radio stations played the song, too.

The recording features a small group of musicians: [[Floyd Cramer]] on piano, Marvin Hughes on the vibraphone, [[Bob Moore (musician)|Bob Moore]] on bass, [[Buddy Harman]] on drums, [[Hank Garland]] on guitar, and the [[Anita Kerr Singers]] providing the background vocals.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://3chordsaday.wordpress.com/2009/10/15/hell-have-to-go-jim-reeves/|title="He'll Have To Go" | Jim Reeves|date=15 October 2009|access-date=26 April 2021}}</ref>

The first verse set the tone: "Put your sweet lips a little closer to the phone/Let's pretend that we're together all alone/I'll tell the man to turn the juke box way down low/And you can tell your friend there with you he'll have to go."<ref name=pc10>{{Gilliland |url=https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark:/67531/metadc19758/m1/ |title=Show 10 - Tennessee Firebird: American country music before and after Elvis. [Part 2]|website=Digital.library.unt.edu }}</ref>

Country music historian Bill Malone noted that "He'll Have to Go" in most respects represented a conventional country song, but its arrangement and the vocal chorus "put this recording in the country pop vein." In addition, Malone lauded Reeves' vocal styling - lowered to "its natural resonant level" to project the "caressing style that became famous" - as being why "many people refer to him as the singer with the velvet touch."<ref>Malone, Bill, "Classic Country Music: A Smithsonian Collection" ((booklet included with  ''[[Classic Country Music: A Smithsonian Collection]]'' 4-disc set). Smithsonian Institution, 1990), p. 51.</ref>

sections.heading: Chart performance
sections.wikitext:
The song reached number two on the [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]] in early 1960, kept from the top spot by [[Percy Faith]]'s "[[Theme from A Summer Place|Theme from ''A Summer Place'']]".{{Cite web|url=https://www.billboard.com/charts/hot-100/1960-03-07|title=The Hot 100 Chart|website=Billboard.com|access-date=26 April 2021}} ''Billboard'' ranked it as the number-two song of the year for 1960. The song also reached number one on the [[Hot Country Singles]] chart on February 8, 1960, where it remained for 14 consecutive weeks.{{cite book |title= The Billboard Book Of Top 40 Country Hits: 1944-2006, Second edition|last=Whitburn |first=Joel |author-link=Joel Whitburn |year=2004 |publisher=Record Research |page=285}} The song was one of just five different titles to occupy the chart's summit during 1960. In addition, it reached number 13 on the [[rhythm and blues]] singles chart.{{cite book |title= Top R&B/Hip-Hop Singles: 1942-2004|last=Whitburn |first=Joel |author-link=Joel Whitburn |year=2004 |publisher=Record Research |page=488}} In Canada, the song was number one for six weeks on the pop charts.{{cite web|url=http://hitsofalldecades.com/chart_hits/index.php?option=com_content&task=view&id=851&Itemid=52|title=RADIO STATION CHUM (TORONTO) WEEKLY CHARTS FOR 1960 | publisher=Barry Kowal - hits of all decades | access-date=23 August 2023}} It also had success abroad, reaching number one on the Australian singles chart and number 12 on the [[UK Singles Chart]].{{Cite web|url=https://www.officialcharts.com/search/singles/he%27ll-have-to-go/|title=he'll have to go | full Official Chart History | Official Charts Company|website=Officialcharts.com|access-date=26 April 2021}} {{col-begin}} {{col-2}} {|class="wikitable sortable" !align="left"|Chart (1960) !align="center"|Peak

sections.heading: Other versions
sections.wikitext:
"He'll Have to Go" has been recorded by many other artists. [[Elvis Presley]] recorded his version of "He'll Have to Go" on October 31, 1976, at his last known studio recording session; it is believed to be the final song he ever recorded in a studio setting.<ref>Ernst Jørgensen, ''Elvis Presley: A Life in Music'' (St; Martin's Press, 1998), p. 400.</ref>

The song prompted the [[answer song]] "[[He'll Have to Stay]]" by [[Jeanne Black]]. Her song reached No. 6 on the ''Billboard'' Hot C&W Sides chart and No. 4 on the ''Billboard'' Hot 100 in 1960.

[[Les Paul]] and [[Mary Ford]] recorded the song as "She'll Have to Go" for their 1962 album ''Bouquet of Roses''.

[[Tom Jones (singer)|Tom Jones]] recorded a version for his 1967 album ''[[Green, Green Grass of Home (album)|Green, Green Grass of Home]]''.

Country music satirists [[Homer and Jethro]] parodied the song on their 1962 live album ''Homer and Jethro at the Convention''.<ref>{{cite web|website=Discogs|url=https://www.discogs.com/release/8070249-Homer-And-Jethro-Homer-And-Jethro-At-The-Convention|title=Homer And Jethro – Homer And Jethro At The Convention|date=1962 |accessdate=August 7, 2023}}</ref>

[[Barry Young (musician)|Barry Young]] reached No. 68 in [[RPM (magazine)|Canada]] with his version in 1966.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.collectionscanada.gc.ca/obj/028020/f2/nlc008388.5753.pdf| title=RPM Top 100 - May 30, 1966}}</ref>

Guitarist [[Ry Cooder]] recorded a version with a Mexican [[Norteño (music)|norteño]]-style arrangement for his 1976 album ''[[Chicken Skin Music]]''.

[[Solomon Burke]] had a crossover hit with his 1964 version of the song on the US Adult Contemporary and R&B charts.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.musicvf.com/songs.php?page=artist&artist=Solomon+Burke|title=Solomon Burke Songs • Top Songs / Chart Singles Discography • Music VF, US & UK hits charts|website=Musicvf.com|access-date=26 April 2021}}</ref>

[[Bryan Ferry]] recorded the song in 1977, but it remained unreleased until 1988 when it was included on the album ''[[The_Ultimate_Collection_(Bryan_Ferry_and_Roxy_Music_album)|The Ultimate Collection]]''.

[[Elton John]] has performed the song several times live, during a variety of solo tours and television appearances, and at various stops on his 1979 tour with [[Ray Cooper]], including the series of shows the two played at the Rossya Hall in Moscow, Russia, the last night of which was broadcast live on BBC Radio.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.eltonography.com/tours/1979.html | title=Elton John Concerts }}</ref>

[[UB40]] recorded the song for their 2013 album ''[[Getting Over the Storm]]''.

The song has also been covered by [[Joe Pesci]], Scottish rocker [[Frankie Miller]], English pop band [[Prefab Sprout]] and English rock band [[the Quireboys]].

In 2023, ''He'll Have to Go'', an [[Independent film|independent short film]] named after the song was released and won the Finalist Award at the SWIFF International Film Festival for Best Short Film.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Instagram |url=https://www.instagram.com/p/CuAadkpsSMI/?igsh=NGh3eTZhcGpoaWlt |access-date=2024-12-22 |website=www.instagram.com}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |last=Wylie |first=Dylan |title=He'll Have to Go |date=2023-03-06 |type=Short, Horror |url=https://www.imdb.com/title/tt27041223/ |access-date=2024-12-22 |others=Micheal Hanna, Paige Mckee, Adam Charles |publisher=Wylie Productions}}</ref>
sections.text:
"He'll Have to Go" has been recorded by many other artists. Elvis Presley recorded his version of "He'll Have to Go" on October 31, 1976, at his last known studio recording session; it is believed to be the final song he ever recorded in a studio setting.

The song prompted the answer song "He'll Have to Stay" by Jeanne Black. Her song reached No. 6 on the Billboard Hot C&W Sides chart and No. 4 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1960.

Les Paul and Mary Ford recorded the song as "She'll Have to Go" for their 1962 album Bouquet of Roses.

Tom Jones recorded a version for his 1967 album Green, Green Grass of Home.

Country music satirists Homer and Jethro parodied the song on their 1962 live album Homer and Jethro at the Convention.

Barry Young reached No. 68 in Canada with his version in 1966.

Guitarist Ry Cooder recorded a version with a Mexican norteño-style arrangement for his 1976 album Chicken Skin Music.

Solomon Burke had a crossover hit with his 1964 version of the song on the US Adult Contemporary and R&B charts.

Bryan Ferry recorded the song in 1977, but it remained unreleased until 1988 when it was included on the album The Ultimate Collection.

Elton John has performed the song several times live, during a variety of solo tours and television appearances, and at various stops on his 1979 tour with Ray Cooper, including the series of shows the two played at the Rossya Hall in Moscow, Russia, the last night of which was broadcast live on BBC Radio.

UB40 recorded the song for their 2013 album Getting Over the Storm.

The song has also been covered by Joe Pesci, Scottish rocker Frankie Miller, English pop band Prefab Sprout and English rock band the Quireboys.

In 2023, He'll Have to Go, an independent short film named after the song was released and won the Finalist Award at the SWIFF International Film Festival for Best Short Film.
